title: David's great wrong (2 Samuel 11)
hookLine: a king on a rooftop takes Bathsheba and arranges her husband's death

lines: WHEN KINGS GO FORTH TO BATTLE.
cards: The chapter opens "at the time when kings go forth to battle," and adds a quiet line: "But David tarried still at Jerusalem."
One evening he gets up from his bed and walks on the palace roof, and from up there he sees a woman bathing. He asks who she is.

The answer comes back with her name and, pointedly, her husband's: Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah the Hittite, one of his soldiers, away at the war. The king knows exactly who she is. And he sends for her anyway.

teach.b: The verbs belong to the king: "David sent messengers, and took her." Sent, took.
Some readers point out that Bathsheba had little room to say no, and the text gives her no words at all until a message she sends back: "I am with child." Then the cover-up.
David calls Uriah home from the war, and sends him off to his house, hoping the child will seem to be his. Uriah sleeps at the palace door with the servants instead.

Asked why, the soldier answers with a loyalty that shames the king: "The ark, and Israel, and Judah, abide in tents; and my lord Joab, and the servants of my lord, are encamped in the open fields; shall I then go into mine house, to eat and to drink, and to lie with my wife?"
David gets him drunk the next night; he still doesn't go home.

So David writes to his general, and has Uriah carry the letter himself: "Set ye Uriah in the forefront of the hottest battle, and retire ye from him, that he may be smitten, and die." Other soldiers die with him.
David sends back a smooth message: don't let this trouble you; the sword devours one as well as another. Then he marries Bathsheba. For a moment it looks like he got away with it.
The chapter's last line says otherwise: "But the thing that David had done displeased the LORD." This is the same man who spared Saul in the cave. The text doesn't explain the change.
Some readers point to how much power he now had, and how few people could tell him no.

how: Some Christians read 2 Samuel 11 as a sobering story about the abuse of power and the way one wrong leads to the next, and read it alongside Nathan's rebuke and Psalm 51.

o: the loyal soldier David had sent to his death
the general who led David's army in the field
the prophet who confronted David over his sin

games.q: the rooftop and the letter — tap the pairs.

s: Uriah went home to his wife when David sent him
he slept at the door of the king's house, because the army was camped in the fields.
David was at the battle when this happened
the chapter ends by saying the thing displeased the LORD

games.q: you're Uriah. the king has called you home from the war and told you to go down to your house. what do you do?
o: go home and rest with your wife.
sleep at the palace door with the servants.
go straight back to the battle.
games.why: he sleeps at the door of the king's house. how can he go home, he says, while the ark and the army are in tents? his loyalty undoes the cover-up.

practice: Hold in mind Bathsheba, who speaks only once in this chapter, and Uriah, carrying his own death warrant without knowing it.
Then let your mind move to people today who have been used or silenced by someone with power over them, at work, at home, in a church; you don't need names.
If you pray, pray for them in your own words or in silence; if not, simply hold them in mind with care.

wordCard.voice: Uriah. The loyal soldier whose wife David took, and whom David then arranged to have killed in battle.

carryVoice: Your line: power can rot. Sent, took: two short verbs, and a long fall. Day seven hundred twenty-three, done.
